plan.topic: Sleeping better or snoring less on Foundayo (orforglipron)? Why you shouldn't drop your CPAP on your own
plan.angle: Hook (14 words or fewer): 'On Foundayo and using CPAP? Keep it until your sleep clinician says otherwise.' Relief fact: 'In two 52-week trials, orforglipron cut breathing interruptions more than placebo did.' Next sentence: 'about 13 fewer an hour than placebo in the trial without CPAP.' Card: 'Adults with moderate to severe sleep apnea, BMI 27+ · one trial with PAP, one without'. Then 'It isn't approved for sleep apnea.', 'If you use CPAP, don't stop or change it on your own.', 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and the loop line. Don't say snoring less or sleeping better, and don't name a drug as a CPAP replacement. Watch-next goes to L1 once it's live, otherwise ssb7Zcs3KSY.
plan.working_title: Foundayo (Orforglipron): Sleeping Better? Keep the CPAP #shorts
plan.why: Spin-off of L1: a practical moment tied to a searched drug name that sends viewers to the long video. | fact-check: This is a safe and useful angle: it tells viewers not to drop prescribed CPAP. The working title 'Sleeping Better?' could suggest the trial measured how people felt or how much they snored. The primary result was AHI, so stay with breathing interruptions and don't claim less snoring or better sleep. Use L1's verified JAMA figures. The cleanest single number is the placebo-adjusted difference: about 13 fewer events an hour in the trial without PAP and about 12 in the trial with PAP, one number per sentence. Population: adults with moderate to severe OSA and a BMI of 27 or more. It is not approved for OSA. This Short depends on L1's verified figures, so wait for L1's content check.

package.title: Orforglipron (Foundayo) Sleep Apnea Trials: Why Not to Drop CPAP on Your Own #shorts
package.description:
In two 52-week trials in adults without diabetes with moderate to severe sleep apnea and a BMI of 27 or more, orforglipron (Foundayo) cut breathing interruptions more than placebo: about 13 fewer an hour in the trial without PAP and about 12 fewer an hour in the trial with PAP, on average. Orforglipron is not approved for sleep apnea. If you use CPAP, don't stop or change it on your own. Ask your sleep clinician.
#Orforglipron
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

script.cta: Post notes: No spoken channel pointer, no subscribe line and no 'link in the description'. Watch-next / related-video target: L1 'Foundayo (Orforglipron) for Sleep Apnea: What Did the Trial Show?' once it is live; until then, Foundayo What to Expect (ssb7Zcs3KSY). Word count, counted by hand: 157 spoken words with hyphenated numbers as one word, or 160 if 'fifty-two-week' and 'twenty-seven' are split. Either way it is inside the standard arm (135–160). How I got there: the s7 fix added 3 words, so I cut s6 'Bring the question to your sleep clinician.' down to 'Ask your sleep clinician.' to keep the split count at 160 or under. All 5 fact-check fixes applied: s1 card and narration, s3 and s4 cards, title, s7 narration. The s3 and s4 stat_labels are trimmed to 8 words; the population is on the on-screen text. S2 uses the verified HTML label URL (printed 'Revised: 7/2026'). Motion note: s1 on-screen text is long, so split it into whole-clause cards and keep 'Not an approved use' on screen from t=0.

factcheck.summary: All claims check out against JAMA ATTAIN-OSA (Malhotra et al., 9 Nov 2026, doi:10.1001/jama.2026.24080) and the Foundayo PI (Revised 7/2026). Trial 1 (no PAP): mean AHI change −17.8 vs −4.5, difference −13.2 events/h. Trial 2 (on PAP and planning to continue): −17.3 vs −5.3, difference −12.0. Both ran 52 weeks in adults with moderate to severe OSA and BMI ≥27, and people with diabetes were excluded. The PI's Section 1 covers weight reduction only, so "not approved for sleep apnea" is correct. Hedges, comparators and population are right on every card. CPAP safety framing is good. The one issue is a word-count error in the post notes, which is minor.
